name: Resonance tuning (formant)

lead: Resonance tuning means adjusting the shape of the throat and mouth so vocal tract resonances, called formants, shift and give the voice a different timbre. Voice-modification communities use it aiming for a deeper, darker or more masculine sound.

Formants are broad peaks in the sound spectrum created by acoustic resonance in the vocal tract, and changes in mouth and lip shape move them; for example, lip rounding lowers them. Vowels are identified mostly by the first two formants. The acoustics is well established, though no studies test deliberate tuning for perceived attractiveness.

paras: People practise with spectrogram or formant-display apps, changing tongue, lip and throat position while recording and comparing the sound. It is typically combined with pitch and breath work over weeks.
No risks are documented in the sources reviewed. As with any vocal practice, pain or hoarseness is a sign to stop.

angle.text: Reshaping the vocal tract moves its resonances, or formants, to give the voice a deeper, darker timbre. Formant acoustics is well established science; its use as a deliberate voice-improvement method has not been tested.

lead: Resonance tuning is the deliberate shaping of the throat, mouth and lips so that the voice's formants, the broad spectral peaks created by acoustic resonance in the vocal tract, move to different frequencies. People use it to change how their voice sounds, for example to make it come across as deeper, warmer, brighter or more projected, without changing the pitch of the vocal folds.[1][2]

Formants shape the sound produced by the voice but are not sound sources themselves. Vowel identity depends largely on the first two formants, and changes in vocal tract length or in lip, tongue and jaw position shift them; lip rounding lowers formants, and a longer tract lowers resonance frequencies.[1] Trained classical singers show an additional peak near 3000 Hz, often called the singer's formant or ring, which gives a voice brilliance and helps it carry over an orchestra.[1][3] A 2016 review notes that humans can voluntarily modulate fundamental and formant frequencies, the features linked to impressions of body size and sex.[4]

In voice training for transgender clients, speech-language pathologists work on resonance alongside pitch because formants strongly influence perceived gender even when fundamental frequency stays the same; techniques described include lip protrusion or retraction, larynx height control and chest resonance work.[5] The same acoustic principles underlie how voice-improvement communities discuss making a voice sound fuller or more resonant, since a voice is part of the impression a person makes.

Singer's formant, vocal resonance, voice therapy

paras: The first formant is higher for open vowels and lower for closed ones, and the second is higher for front vowels; lip rounding lowers both. Changes in vocal tract length scale all resonance frequencies.[1]

Vocal resonance in general is described as enhancement of the voice's basic sound by the air-filled spaces it passes through, changing timbre or intensity. The pharynx is described as the most important resonator because of its position, size and adjustability, while the tongue, jaw and lips reshape the oral cavity and act as a final filter. These supraglottal structures are under voluntary control, whereas the larynx is not directly consciously controlled.[2]

Voice teachers describe a range of colours from dark, chest-based resonance to bright, head and nasal resonance. Chest resonance is said to add warmth and depth, nasal resonance brightness and projection, and mouth resonance a conversational colour.[2]

In voice therapy for transgender people, vocal tract length is used to explain perceived pitch: a male vocal tract is described as 10 to 20 percent longer than a female one, giving lower resonance. Clients are taught lip retraction to shorten the tract, or larynx lowering and chest resonance to deepen the sound, and semi-occluded exercises such as phonating through a straw.[5]

Fundamental frequency and resonance are described as the changes with the greatest effect on perceived gender, and clients who complete voice therapy report high satisfaction. A 2012 review cited there rated the evidence base as weak, with most studies at the lowest level of the evidence hierarchy.[5]
No studies found testing resonance tuning specifically as an appearance or attractiveness practice. Related research on voice resonance exists in voice therapy and singing, as described above.[5]
